title: Free Heavy-Tailed Lunch for Muon: A Theoretical Justification of Empirical Success
claim: Measured noise-geometry ratios in real training stay well below the worst-case bound, so the theoretical dimension penalty is pessimistic.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, dashed worst-case line atop both
description: Two side-by-side scatter plots share a y-axis labelled σ_S1/σ_S2, ranging from about 4 to 23. Each dot is one weight matrix of a trained Transformer. Dots are coloured by weight family: blue att.qkv, orange att.out, red mlp.up, purple mlp.down. Within each family they are ordered left to right by layer depth, and faint dotted vertical lines separate the families. A dashed red horizontal line near 22.5 marks the worst-case ratio. A solid black line marks the mean ratio. Panel (a), at initialisation, has a mean near 8.5. Attention dots cluster low at 4–7, while MLP dots sit at 11–16. Panel (b), at the final checkpoint, has a mean near 12.8. Dots are more spread out, from 7 to 19, and rise with depth. In both panels every dot sits well below the red dashed line. The eye goes first to the red line and then to the gap beneath it.
caption: Ratios σS1,p/σF,p for p = 1.5 across all weight matrices trained by MUON. Colours indicate weight families, ordered by layer depth within. While non-trivial, the noise ratios stay considerably below the worst-case ratio
abstract: Non-Euclidean optimisation methods with matrix-valued updates, such as Muon and Scion, have recently shown strong empirical performance for training Transformer models, yet their theoretical advantages over Euclidean methods remain poorly understood. We address this gap in the heavy-tailed non-convex regime, where stochastic gradients have bounded $p$-th central moments, $p \in (1,2]$. We show that certain non-Euclidean methods achieve optimal sample complexity under stronger stationarity measures, while Euclidean methods incur additional dimension-dependent costs. As a consequence, for $m \times n$ matrices, Muon finds an $\varepsilon$-stationary point in nuclear norm within $\mathcal{O}\left(\min\{m, n\} \frac{Î_1 L}{\varepsilon^2} \left(\frac Ï\varepsilon \right)^{\frac p {p-1}}\right)$ samples, absorbing heavy-tailed noise without extra dimension dependence, unlike Euclidean methods. We further prove this sample complexity, including its dimension dependence, is optimal for all first-order methods under nuclear-norm stationarity. Experiments on large language models support our theory. Surprisingly, our results suggest that other Schatten geometries beyond the spectral geometry of Muon can perform competitively in certain settings.
